THREE-MONTH ROADMAP / TIME TO 10.0

Purpose: this is a local planning clock, not a promise of autonomous background work. It tracks the path from the current verified engineering baseline to a measurable 10.0 release target while protecting sound continuity first.

MONTH 1 / OBSERVE + STABILIZE
Repair diagnostics reachability, session checkpoints, controlled long-set logging, audio-context recovery, memory ceilings, and representative acceptance packs. No new aggressive audio processing is promoted before continuity stays green.

MONTH 2 / UNDERSTAND + SCORE
Add phrase/section evidence, transition contribution scoring, beat-phase and stereo stability checks, vocal-versus-instrument confidence, and explainable before/after reports. Every score must show confidence and a safe fallback.

MONTH 3 / BENCHMARK + PROMOTE
Run blinded human-versus-Auto-DJ comparisons on the same track pairs, calibrate thresholds from real listening, promote only improvements that beat the baseline without increasing silence, clipping, drift, crashes, or lyric masking, then freeze a 10.0 candidate release.
10.0 SCORECARD
Continuity 2.0 · loudness stability 1.0 · transition smoothness 1.0 · beat/phrase timing 1.0 · vocal clarity 1.0 · harmonic safety 0.75 · explainability 0.75 · resource stability 1.0 · reversible editing 0.75 · human-listening benchmark 0.75.
Current status: technically strong in continuity, recovery, bounded loudness, and observability; not yet proven 10/10 and not proven superior to an expert human DJ.
❓ HOW THIS WORKS — tap to read

Fastest path: drop a folder of tracks into LIBRARY below, then tap GO. It analyzes everything, builds a beatmatched play order, and runs the whole set unattended — crossfading track to track on its own.

LIBRARY — bulk-drop audio files. Each new track runs five bounded preparation scans before it becomes deck-ready, then the compact result is cached in this browser. The scans are: 1) REFERENCE + HIGH-PASS for safe level reference, headroom, and detector-only subsonic cleanup; 2) BASS / MID / PROBLEM CONTROL for band-specific dominance, masking, and harshness evidence; 3) MUSICAL / EDIT DECISION for vocal compression, section EQ, target window, tempo direction, and conservative edit candidates; 4) QUIET / LOUD DYNAMIC EQ REVIEW for the track's own changing energy; and 5) RHYTHM / SILENCE PATTERN for beat-linked returns without boosting silence. Deck loading then builds the full STFT-backed adaptive EQ map at roughly 23ms control spacing and applies it with bounded smoothing. Reloading the same file later can reuse its cached result.

WORK MODE — choose AUTO DJ / PROTECTED PLAYBACK for unattended sets or DAW / SAFE EDIT for reversible preparation and auditioning. DAW mode refuses GO and Auto DJ starts, protects build/drop structure, does not rewrite source audio, and keeps every edit bounded and undoable in the decision log.

GO — one-tap autonomous set over your (optionally filtered) library. Turns AUTO DJ on and keeps pulling the next best-matching track into whichever deck frees up as the set runs. Every library-prepared track receives three additional lightweight micro-scans at deck entry before its small handoff adjustments are applied.

ADVANCED / MANUAL CONTROLS — open this to see the two decks directly: waveform, spectrogram heatmap, live BPM/dance stats, manual play/stop, and the crossfader. It also has:

  • AUTO DJ — the same beatmatching GO uses, but only blends between whatever you've manually loaded on A/B (no queue behind it).
  • HOOK MODE — plays only each track's detected highest-energy window instead of start-to-finish. In full-track Auto DJ mode, a high-confidence prepared track may use a roughly two-minute preferred window and skip only a sustained low-value candidate outside the hook window. Possible glitches are flagged for inspection rather than destructively deleted.
  • FIND BEST PAIRS / RUBRIC RANK — score every combination, or every single track, for DJ-readiness.
  • FILTERS — narrow the library by BPM range, minimum danceability, or a tag before GO or FIND BEST PAIRS runs.
  • EXPORT FINGERPRINT JSON — dump the analysis numbers for whatever's loaded on A/B right now.
  • CUES — reveal compact, confidence-scored intro, hook, build-up, drop, low-value candidate, and outro markers from the preparation evidence. These are audition candidates, not destructive edits.
  • EXPORT LIBRARY CUE MAP — save the whole library's compact cue candidates as local JSON for a producer or controller workflow.

PREPARATION is level-safe and non-destructive. BAD-D may lift a quiet track only to a bounded internal analysis reference, never to full-scale loudness. Its high-pass and bass reduction are detector-side-chain operations used to expose problems; the audible source keeps its shape. The mid band returns to a neutral reference before narrow or broad corrections are chosen. Dynamic-style cuts are preferred over broad boosts when a band becomes overbearing. At deck entry, the three micro-scans repeat this reference → band/vocal → musical safety sequence. If no singing is likely, the system may apply a very small low/high support and mid reduction; if a beat is not safely aligned, it prefers a fade-safe entry.

DAW-SAFE PRODUCER RULES — build-ups and drops are protected; no destructive crop is performed; possible glitches and boring passages remain candidates; room size, close/far vocal character, and atmosphere width are heuristics from spectral and energy evidence, not a substitute for stems or a real room model. Harmonic clashes are reduced or faded, never boosted merely because they are clashes. If a transition is stopped before completion, its temporary loudness, EQ, duck, and filter moves are cancelled and restored before the next run, so an interrupted handoff cannot quietly accumulate attenuation. A conservative sibilance heuristic watches 4–10 kHz energy only when vocal evidence is strong; it is not a word, letter, male/female timbre, or stem detector, and it applies at most a small high-band cut.

KEY stat on each deck — the track's detected musical key and Camelot wheel code (e.g. "8A · A min"). GO, AUTO DJ and FIND BEST PAIRS all now factor harmonic (in-key) compatibility into their match scoring, not just BPM/energy/dance.

🎤 LYRICS ENGINE — optional, one-time ~40MB in-browser model download. Once loaded, tap LYRICS on a track to transcribe it; matching words at the transition point slightly boost that pair's mix score.

☰ menu (top right) — loop the set, see the current set's match score, and download a JSON time-map of every load/transition/score this session.

🧠 CLAUDE TUNING — optional copy/paste tuning only. BAD-D generates a compact session summary locally; you can copy it into a Claude conversation, review the response yourself, and paste the suggested bounded tuning reply back into BAD-D. Automatic outbound consultation is disabled in this stable build, and no API key is required or stored. Audio, source tracks, and raw event logs remain local.

DJ PRACTICE BEHIND THE AUTOMATION — the system borrows durable DJ ideas: cueing and downbeats, beatmatching, nudging, phrasing, EQ/fader blending, harmonic compatibility, loops, and controlled effects. It also recognizes modern preparation patterns such as waveform/cue analysis, smart transitions, library ranking, stems as a future gated capability, and controller integration as a future work item.

Everything else runs locally in this tab. No audio ever leaves your device.

Operator mode hides manual deck edits and diagnostics without changing audio, queue, or analysis behavior.

there's no reliable way for a browser tab to detect this automatically — no cross-platform API exists, and the ones that come close would need mic permission for something unrelated. this is manual, but it's not cosmetic: on "phone speaker," bass-collision warnings get discounted, because a phone speaker can't reproduce most of the frequency range a bass collision lives in — no point ducking hard to fix a problem that speaker was never going to play.
off by default. GO normally just chains whichever compatible track scores best next, forever — no sense of the set as a whole. This nudges that choice toward a classic arc instead: lower-energy tracks early, peak around 60% through, easing down for the close. It's a bias on top of the same compatibility scoring, not a replacement for it — a bad match still won't get picked just because its energy fits the curve.
— run GO to generate a set —
the RUN ARCHIVE is the big evidence dump: it keeps the raw session ledger plus bounded autonomous signal samples and read-only module summaries in one JSON file, so another tool can compress/analyse the run without making you stare at BAD-D. The older time-map remains available for the smaller legacy workflow.
nothing is sent anywhere automatically and no API key is stored in this app. Copy the prompt below, paste it into any Claude conversation yourself (claude.ai, the app, whatever you use), then paste Claude's reply back in to apply it.
The copy/paste flow above remains available. Automatic outbound consultation is disabled so queue errors cannot trigger repeated paid requests. No key is needed for local playback or analysis.
the copied prompt includes a compact summary of this session (average bpm/energy/dance match, how often it synced, which EQ technique it used, and the two weakest-matched pairs) and the app's current weight settings, and asks Claude for a short critique plus small weight nudges — never your audio, and never a raw event-by-event log. accepted nudges are clamped to small steps and saved in this browser, so the app's mixing gets tuned a little more each time you do this, across sessions.

groups tracks by measured character (role, tempo, brightness) — useful when filenames give you no clue what a track actually is. this isn't genre detection; BAD-D doesn't have a genre classifier, so it doesn't guess one. these are the real, measurable dimensions it can actually back up.
exact audio duplicates (same content, different filename — usually a browser "(1)" re-download) can be removed in one tap. same-title tracks with different audio (remix/remaster passes) are listed for you to review — those might be intentional keepers, so nothing there gets removed automatically.
